title: Price & Performance
text: Does paying more for a car always buy you a stronger engine, or are buyers mostly paying for body style and badge prestige? Across nearly ten thousand vehicles, we look at how horsepower and sticker price move together—focusing on engine horsepower since public specification sources leave torque unrecorded.

title: Price & Performance
section: Horsepower vs. Price by Body Style
text:
Horsepower vs. Price by Body Style









Figure 1





More horsepower pushes prices upward in every category, but two-door sporty cars climb much faster than everyday family or work vehicles. Coupes and convertibles shoot steeply into luxury territory as power rises, while pickups and minivans pack strong towing engines without the steep luxury markup. Economy hatchbacks stay clustered in the most affordable, lower-powered corner of the market. (Ultra-rare hypercars above $250k are set aside here so everyday price trends stay easy to read.)

title: Price & Performance
text:
Best Horsepower Value by Brand









Figure 2





Mainstream automakers deliver far more raw muscle per dollar than luxury or exotic badges. Everyday brands like Dodge, Kia, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and Ford sit right at the top because they offer strong engines at approachable prices, whereas European luxury and supercar makers sit near the bottom—showing that high-end buyers pay heavily for interior craftsmanship, handling, and prestige rather than cheap horsepower.

title: Price & Performance
text:
Average Price by Body Style









Figure 3





Convertibles and coupes cost roughly twice as much on average as any other body style, largely because almost all exotic sports cars and grand tourers are built with two doors. Practical styles—including sedans, SUVs, pickups, wagons, minivans, and hatchbacks—stay much closer to mainstream family budgets, with hatchbacks serving as the most affordable entry point.

title: Price & Performance
section: A Note on Historical Prices vs. Newer Cars
text:
A Note on Historical Prices vs. Newer Cars
Because public specification tables for recent 2022–2027 models do not publish sticker prices, the price charts on this page draw from verified 2001–2017 vehicle MSRPs while our other tabs explore newer 2022–2027 models directly. Since 2017, new-car prices and turbo/electric horsepower have both climbed noticeably, so these charts best capture how brands and body styles position themselves relative to one another rather than today’s exact showroom sticker tags.

title: Automotive Trends
text: Today’s vehicles look almost nothing like the cars on American roads fifty years ago. Long-term U.S. Environmental Protection Agency records show how automakers responded to fuel crises, changing family tastes, and modern clean-energy rules—transforming heavy, thirsty sedans of the 1970s into today’s lineup of turbocharged crossovers, pickups, hybrids, and electric vehicles.

title: Automotive Trends
section: Doubling Efficiency and Horsepower Over Time
text:
Doubling Efficiency and Horsepower Over Time









Figure 1





American cars moved through three clear eras over the past half-century. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, automakers boosted gas mileage quickly by shrinking heavy cars and trimming engine output. For the next twenty years, fuel economy plateaued because new engine gains went straight into bigger SUVs and stronger engines instead. Only over the last two decades—thanks to turbocharging, modern transmissions, hybrids, and electric motors—have both fuel economy and horsepower climbed together to record highs.

title: Automotive Trends
section: How SUVs Replaced the Family Sedan
text:
How SUVs Replaced the Family Sedan









Figure 2





In the mid-1970s, sedans and station wagons dominated American driveways while SUVs were a tiny niche. Over the decades that followed, minivans briefly surged before crossovers and truck-based SUVs steadily took over the market—until SUVs now represent roughly three out of every five new vehicles built, leaving traditional sedans at an all-time low while pickup trucks hold a steady, loyal slice of the market.

title: Automotive Trends
section: Vehicle Weight and Tailpipe Carbon Today
text:
Vehicle Weight and Tailpipe Carbon Today









Figure 3





Among recent gasoline and diesel vehicles, extra weight carries a clear environmental cost: heavier trucks and large SUVs burn more fuel per mile and release far more tailpipe carbon than compact cars and hybrids. Battery-electric models break that weight penalty at the tailpipe—forming a flat zero-emission line across the bottom of the chart from compact hatchbacks all the way up to heavy electric pickups.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text: Today’s car shoppers choose between traditional fuel engines, hybrids, and pure battery-electric vehicles. Looking across recent 2022–2027 models, we compare how each powertrain handles city traffic versus open-highway cruising, which electric brands travel farthest on a single charge, and how much drivers actually spend on fuel or electricity each year.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
City Traffic vs. Highway Cruising









Figure 1





Gasoline and diesel cars sit above the dashed diagonal line because their engines run more efficiently at steady highway speeds than in stop-and-go traffic. Electric vehicles flip that pattern completely, sitting below the line because regenerative braking recaptures energy every time the driver slows down in the city while wind resistance works hardest on the highway. Conventional hybrids bridge the middle, delivering nearly even efficiency everywhere.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
Single-Charge Range Across Electric Brands









Figure 2





Focusing strictly on pure battery-electric cars reveals two very different engineering paths to long driving range. Sleek sedan specialists like Lucid and Tesla pair long driving distances with bright-red high efficiency through low weight and smooth aerodynamics, whereas electric truck makers like Chevrolet, Rivian, and GMC reach long range by fitting huge, heavy battery packs that draw noticeably more electricity per mile.

title: Fuel Economy & EV Range
text:
Yearly Fuel and Electricity Costs









Figure 3





Those efficiency gains show up directly in owners’ wallets. Pure electric vehicles cost roughly a quarter as much to power each year as traditional gasoline or diesel models, saving typical drivers thousands of dollars over several years of ownership, while hybrids offer meaningful yearly pump savings for drivers without home charging.
